traveler: Aurelius Augustinus, Saint Augustine of Hippo
title: Thagaste to the Golden Sky: the Rhetor, the Garden at Milan, and the Bones That Kept Moving
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Thagaste, the birth in a councillor's small house
stops.date_confidence: attested: 13 November 354, per the New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia and the standard chronology
stops.campa: A son is born at Thagaste in Roman Numidia, an inland market town of grain and olives, and is named Aurelius Augustinus. His father Patricius holds a few fields and a seat on the town council and is not baptized; he will take the water only in the last months of his life. His mother Monnica, born about 331, is a Catholic Christian of the ordinary stubborn sort. The house speaks Latin and hears Punic in the fields. The schooling Patricius intends for the boy will cost more than the fields bring in.
stops.quote: Great are You, O Lord, and greatly to be praised; great is Your power, and of Your wisdom there is no end.
stops.quote_source: Augustine, Confessions I.1, tr. J. G. Pilkington, NPNF First Series vol. 1
suggested_refs: The site of Roman Thagaste under modern Souk Ahras, Algeria
sources: New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia, 'St. Augustine of Hippo'

stops.name: Thagaste, the schoolroom and the baptism put off
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Confessions I.11 and I.14 give no year, and the illness and deferred baptism are placed conventionally in the Thagaste school years, c. 360-365. Self-testimony with no independent witness
stops.campa: Enrolled as a catechumen and signed with the cross, the boy takes a stomach fever and begs to be baptized. Preparations begin. He recovers, and Monica puts the sacrament off, on the reasoning the age favors, that sins committed after the washing weigh heavier than sins committed before. In the same years he is beaten at school for preferring play to his letters, and prays in earnest not to be beaten. The prayers are not granted. His parents laugh at the welts, and he is still counting the laughter forty years later.
suggested_refs: Confessions I.11, the deferred baptism of the sick boy

stops.name: Madauros, Virgil and the pagan town
stops.date_confidence: traditional: c. 365-369, per the standard biographical timeline; no exact year is attested
stops.campa: Thirty kilometres south, in a town thick with old gods and older statues, the boy is put to grammar and Latin letters. Virgil above all, learned by heart, scanned, declaimed, wept over. Madauros gives him meter, rhetoric, the pagan festival calendar of a Numidian market town, and teachers he will credit and resent in the same sentence. He weeps for Dido on her pyre, burning for a man who sailed. He does not weep for himself. The disproportion is still bothering him when he is an old bishop with a diocese to run.
suggested_refs: The ruins of Madauros at M'Daourouch, Algeria
The Aeneid as the fourth-century grammar-school text
sources: Augustine, Confessions I.13 (weeping for Dido: real but not re-verified in this pass, tagged R in the report)

stops.name: Thagaste, the year at home and the pear tree
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Confessions II places the idle year at age sixteen, 369-370. The pear theft is self-testimony with no witness; the pool's two lenses disagreed over the tag and the report records the disagreement
stops.campa: The money runs out. Patricius, straining to send his son on to Carthage, keeps him home a year, and the boy runs loose in the streets with his gang. One night they strip a neighbour's pear tree of fruit nobody wants and throw most of it to the pigs. There are better pears at home; he says so himself. That is the whole difficulty. He loved the theft and not the pears. What was it he wanted? He is still putting the question decades later, and the Confessions do not answer it.
suggested_refs: Confessions II, the pear tree as a study in gratuitous will

segments.name: Carthage: The Hearer and the School of Rhetoric

stops.name: Carthage, arrival at seventeen
stops.date_confidence: attested: 371, per Britannica and Wikipedia. Pin is Byrsa hill, the fixed landmark used for the ancient city
stops.campa: Romanianus, a rich man of Thagaste, pays what Patricius cannot, and the boy goes down to Carthage for advanced rhetoric. The city hands him everything at once: courts, theatres where he learns to enjoy other people's grief from a safe seat, a cauldron of unholy loves, and four religions arguing in the street. He is quick and ambitious and stands at the head of the rhetoric school inside a year or two. Patricius dies about now, baptized at the last. The Confessions give the death two clauses and move on.
suggested_refs: The Byrsa hill and the Roman theatre of Carthage

stops.name: Carthage, the woman with no name
stops.date_confidence: attested as self-report, Confessions IV; the year is approximate and the month is a placeholder. The woman's name is recorded nowhere in any ancient source
stops.campa: He takes one woman and keeps her, faithfully, for some fourteen years. No source gives her name: not Augustine, not Possidius, not a letter, not a line. She bears him a son about a year later and they call him Adeodatus, given by God, a name Punic families used and Christian families liked. He will describe the arrangement afterwards as a bargain struck by appetite rather than a marriage, which is a verdict on himself. Of her he says only two things: that he was faithful to her, and that the tearing left a wound.
stops.quote: Grant me chastity and continency, but not yet.
stops.quote_source: Augustine, Confessions VIII.7, tr. J. G. Pilkington, NPNF First Series vol. 1, recalling the prayer of his Carthage years
suggested_refs: Confessions IV and VI.15, the only record of the household
sources: Augustine, Confessions IV, VI.15 and VIII.7

stops.name: Carthage, the Hortensius takes the top off his life
stops.date_confidence: attested as self-report: Confessions III.4, in his nineteenth year
stops.campa: In the ordinary course of the syllabus he is handed a dialogue of Cicero called the Hortensius, an exhortation to philosophy, and it changes what he wants. He stops wanting eloquence for its own sake and starts wanting wisdom, a different appetite and a worse-paid one. The Hortensius itself is lost; what survives of it survives because Augustine and men like him quoted it. He turns to the Christian scriptures next, expecting something comparable, and finds a Latin so rough and undignified that he shuts the book.
suggested_refs: Cicero's lost Hortensius, reconstructed from quotation

stops.name: Carthage, the hearer
stops.date_confidence: attested: Confessions III to V; the nine years of attachment are Augustine's own count, running c. 373 to 382. His later account of Manichaean doctrine is a polemicist's, as the scholarship notes
stops.campa: The Manichaeans take him. They have an answer to the thing that will not leave him alone, which is where evil comes from: two eternal substances, Light and Darkness, at war since before the world, and the soul a splinter of Light caught in matter and not to blame for what it suffers there. They also mock the Catholic Bible's seams with a precision he enjoys. He never rises past auditor, the outer rank that may marry and eat meat, and he brings his friends in behind him. Nine years.
suggested_refs: The Manichaean auditor's rank and its rule of life
sources: New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia, 'St. Augustine of Hippo'

stops.name: Thagaste, teaching grammar, and a friend dies
stops.date_confidence: corrected: he taught at Thagaste 373-374 and the friend died in that period, c. 374. The chronology lens dated the death to 376 and the geography lens placed it at Carthage; Confessions IV puts it in his native town and makes the grief the reason he then left for Carthage
stops.campa: He comes home to teach, the first paid use of the education his family bled for, and here he acquires a very dear friend of his own age whom he has drawn after him into the sect. The friend takes fever, is baptized unconscious, wakes, rebukes Augustine for joking about the water, and is dead within days. Grief turns out to be a place before it is a feeling: Augustine cannot stay in a town where every street is the absence of one person. He gives up the school, leaves Thagaste, and goes down to Carthage.
suggested_refs: Confessions IV, the death of the unnamed friend at Thagaste

stops.name: Carthage, the school of rhetoric and the lost book
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Carthage school ran nine years, 375-383. De pulchro et apto is dated only by inference inside that span; the pool's 380 is a placeholder
stops.campa: For nine years he runs a school of rhetoric at Carthage, drilling the sons of the province in persuasion while his own convictions come apart underneath him. He writes his first book here, two or three volumes On the Beautiful and the Fitting, and sends it to Hierius, a Roman orator he has never met and badly wants to be admired by. Nothing in the record says Hierius answered. The book is lost. Decades later Augustine cannot remember whether it ran to two books or three, and says so.
suggested_refs: De pulchro et apto, lost; Confessions IV.13-15 is the only account of it

stops.name: Carthage, Faustus of Milevis has no answer
stops.date_confidence: attested as self-report, Confessions V; reachable sources date the visit to 382 or to 383 and do not agree
stops.campa: The famous Manichaean bishop comes at last to Carthage, and Augustine has been saving questions for years: the eclipses, the solstices, the arithmetic of the sky that the astronomers get right and the sect's books get wrong. Faustus turns out to be charming, well spoken, and honest enough to say that he does not know and has not studied it. The honesty is fatal. Augustine keeps the friendship and quietly stops believing, and writes later that the snare he was caught in had begun to loosen without his hand.
suggested_refs: Augustine's later Contra Faustum Manichaeum, written from Hippo
sources: New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia, 'St. Augustine of Hippo'

stops.name: Carthage, the sailing by night
stops.date_confidence: attested as self-report: 383, Confessions V.8. The month is a placeholder and the harbour chapel where Monica prayed is not locatable, so the pin is the city
stops.campa: His Carthaginian students riot in class and pay when they feel like paying, so he settles on Rome, where the young are said to be disciplined. Monica will not have it. She follows him down to the water and refuses to go home without him, so he tells her he is only seeing a friend off on the tide, and leaves her praying the night through in a chapel by the harbour. The wind comes up and he sails. She wakes to an empty berth, complains of him and prays for him in the same breath, and walks back up the shore to the city.
suggested_refs: The commercial harbour of Roman Carthage

segments.name: Rome and Milan: The Imperial Chair

stops.name: Rome, the fever and the prefect's letter
stops.date_confidence: attested: the illness is Confessions V.9, the Milan appointment 384 per Confessions V.13 and Britannica. No address for Augustine's Roman lodging is recorded anywhere, so the pin is the historic centre
stops.campa: Manichaean contacts find him a house and a first set of students. He falls ill at once, a fever heavy enough that he thinks he is dying, and dying unbaptized. Then he learns what Roman students do instead of rioting: they attend faithfully all term and transfer to another teacher on the day the fees fall due. Meanwhile Milan writes asking the prefect of the city for a court rhetorician. Symmachus, the most eloquent pagan in Rome, sets him a test speech, approves it, and sends him north at public expense.
suggested_refs: Symmachus's own Relatio on the Altar of Victory, written the same year

stops.name: Milan, the most visible chair in the Latin world
stops.date_confidence: attested: he took up the chair in late 384. The month is conventional and the pin is the city centre
stops.campa: He arrives in the effective capital of the western empire with a state salary and the most visible academic post in Latin. The job is to teach declamation and to praise the court in public on demand, in the right meter, on the right day. He is thirty. He keeps a household of mother, son, brother and friends, and is angling for a provincial governorship by way of a rich marriage. Everything he has ever wanted is inside two years' reach. He writes afterwards that he was miserable and dragging his chain.
suggested_refs: The imperial court at Milan under Valentinian II

stops.name: Milan, the cathedral and the bishop's voice
stops.date_confidence: attested that he heard Ambrose preach, Confessions V-VI; the building is inferred. The pin is Ambrose's cathedral on the site of the present Duomo, not the Basilica Martyrum he was then building in a burial ground, which was never his see
stops.campa: He goes to hear Ambrose the way one professional goes to hear another, listening for technique and indifferent to the content. The content gets in anyway. Ambrose reads the Old Testament figuratively, and the crude bodily God the Manichaeans had taught him to laugh at simply dissolves; nine years of objections turn out to be objections to a reading nobody defends. He notices something else about the bishop and cannot account for it: Ambrose reads silently, eyes moving down the page, lips still, alone in a room full of people.
suggested_refs: The Basilica Nova of Milan, Ambrose's cathedral, beneath the present Duomo
sources: Wikipedia, 'Basilica of Sant'Ambrogio' (for the correction: it was the Basilica Martyrum, not the see)

stops.name: Milan, the panegyric and the drunk beggar
stops.date_confidence: attested: Confessions VI.6 gives the occasion as a panegyric on the emperor and names no emperor. The identification with Valentinian II is a scholarly inference, and one of the 385 panegyrics was for the consul Bauto. Month is a placeholder
stops.campa: Walking through Milan working up a formal speech in praise of the emperor, a speech he knows to be mostly lies that his audience knows to be mostly lies, he passes a beggar who has got hold of some money and is drunk and joking and entirely happy. Augustine stops in the street. The beggar's cheerfulness cost a few coins and some begging; his own has cost years of anxious lying and is not cheerfulness at all. He puts the comparison to his friends as they walk. Then he goes and delivers the speech.
suggested_refs: Confessions VI.6, the panegyric and the beggar

stops.name: Milan, Monica arrives and the woman is sent back
stops.date_confidence: attested as self-report, Confessions VI and VI.15; the year is 385 and no month is recorded on either side of it
stops.campa: Monica crosses the sea and takes over the household, bringing Navigius and finding Alypius already installed. She arranges the marriage her son's career requires: a girl of the right family, two years short of legal age, so the wedding must wait. The woman he has lived with for fourteen years is put on a ship to Africa without him, leaving Adeodatus behind, and vows never to know another man. He writes that his heart was cut and wounded and trailed blood. He also writes that, unable to wait two years, he took another woman.
suggested_refs: Confessions VI.15; her name, her family, and the rest of her life are unrecorded

stops.name: Milan, the books of the Platonists
stops.date_confidence: attested as self-report, Confessions VII; the month is a placeholder. The identification of the books with Plotinus and Porphyry in the Latin of Marius Victorinus is standard scholarly reconstruction, not Augustine's statement
stops.campa: A certain man swollen with monstrous pride, as Augustine describes the go-between, puts into his hands some books of the Platonists turned out of Greek into Latin. In them he finds what he had not been able to think: that God need not be a body, need not be extended through space like a sea with the world floating in it, and that evil is not a substance at all but a lack, a turning away, a wound in something good. What he does not find in them is the Word made flesh. He marks the place where the two accounts part.
suggested_refs: Confessions VII; the libri Platonicorum are named nowhere in the text

stops.name: Milan, Simplicianus, Ponticianus, and the two officials at Trier
stops.date_confidence: attested as self-report, Confessions VIII.2 and VIII.6; no months are recorded and the ordering follows Augustine's own narrative. Antony of Egypt never met Augustine and the link runs only through this secondhand telling
stops.campa: The old priest Simplicianus tells him how Marius Victorinus, whose translations he has been reading, once stood up in a Roman church and said the creed aloud in front of everyone, having held it privately for years. Then Ponticianus, an African at court, finds a book of Paul's letters lying on the gaming table and tells them about Antony in the Egyptian desert, and about two colleagues at Trier who read a life of Antony one afternoon and never went back to their posts. Every one of these stories is of a man who turned inside a day. Augustine has been meaning to for years.
suggested_refs: Athanasius, Life of Antony, in the Latin version circulating at Trier

stops.name: Milan, the garden and the child's voice
stops.date_confidence: attested only as self-testimony: Confessions VIII.12, written eleven to fourteen years after the fact, with no witness on record but Alypius. Conventionally dated to late summer 386
stops.campa: He goes out into the small garden of the lodging, Alypius following in silence, and comes apart under a fig tree, weeping and shouting at himself: how long, how long, tomorrow and tomorrow. From a house nearby a child's voice, boy or girl he cannot tell, chants a phrase over and over as if it were a game. He takes it for a command, goes back to the bench where the book is lying, opens Paul at the first place his eye falls, and reads to the end of the sentence. Alypius reads the verse after it, and says nothing.
stops.quote: Take up and read; take up and read.
stops.quote_source: Augustine, Confessions VIII.12, tr. J. G. Pilkington, NPNF First Series vol. 1
suggested_refs: Romans 13:13-14, the verse under his finger

stops.name: Milan, the chair resigned on the grounds of his lungs
stops.date_confidence: corrected: autumn 386, after the vintage vacation and before Cassiciacum. The geography lens gave early 387, which would put the resignation after the retreat and reverse the sequence; New Advent and Confessions IX give autumn 386, and lungs rather than chest and throat
stops.campa: The vintage holidays are close, so he waits them out rather than walking off the job in front of the whole city. Then he resigns the chair on the grounds of his lungs, which really are bad: he has trouble breathing and pains in the chest and can no longer carry a long declamation to the end. The excuse is true and is not the reason. Nobody in Milan is obliged to notice that anything has happened at all. He hands back what he now calls the sale of talk.
suggested_refs: Confessions IX.2, the resignation and the vintage vacation
sources: New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia, 'St. Augustine of Hippo'

stops.name: Cassiciacum, the borrowed villa
stops.date_confidence: the retreat and the four works are attested (Confessions IX.4; New Advent bibliography). The site is not: the identification of Cassiciacum with Cassago Brianza is traditional and disputed, so this pin is provisional
stops.campa: Verecundus, a Milanese grammarian not yet a Christian and unhappy about it, lends his country place, and Augustine takes his mother, his son, his brother, Alypius and two paying pupils out of the city for the autumn and the winter. They argue in the bath house when it rains and in the meadow when it does not, and a shorthand writer takes it down. Four books come out of that season: Against the Academics, On the Happy Life, On Order, and the Soliloquies, in which he asks himself questions and writes down his own answers.
suggested_refs: The Cassiciacum dialogues; the traditional site at Cassago Brianza, Lombardy
sources: New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia, bibliography of Augustine's works

stops.name: Milan, the font beneath the cathedral
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Easter vigil of 387, Confessions IX.6, Britannica, New Advent. The octagonal font of San Giovanni alle Fonti belongs to Ambrose's own episcopate, late fourth century; the 335 date in the pool attaches to a different baptistery, Santo Stefano alle Fonti, and the specific font is a traditional identification
stops.campa: At the Easter vigil Ambrose baptizes the three of them together: the professor, his fifteen-year-old son, and Alypius, who has been walking barefoot on frozen Italian ground as a discipline. Augustine says he wept at the hymns and the voices of the church and that the truth distilled into his heart. A later story has Ambrose and Augustine composing the Te Deum aloud between them at the font, verse answering verse. The story surfaces centuries afterwards and no early source knows anything about it.
stops.quote: Too late did I love You, O Fairness, so ancient, and yet so new! Too late did I love You!
stops.quote_source: Augustine, Confessions X.27, tr. J. G. Pilkington, NPNF First Series vol. 1
suggested_refs: The Battistero di San Giovanni alle Fonti beneath Milan Cathedral

segments.name: Ostia, and the Road Back to Africa

stops.name: Ostia, the window on the garden
stops.date_confidence: attested only as self-testimony, Confessions IX.10, with no external witness. Autumn 387; the month is a placeholder
stops.campa: Waiting at the Tiber mouth for a ship to Africa, mother and son lean together at a window over the courtyard garden and talk about what the eternal life of the saints could possibly be like. The talk climbs as they speak: bodies first, then the sun and the moon, then their own minds, then past minds altogether, and for one beat of the heart they touch the Wisdom by which all these things are made. Then they fall back into the noise of their own mouths, where a word begins and has to end.
suggested_refs: Confessions IX.10, the passage called the vision at Ostia

stops.name: Ostia, the fever, and the grave far from Thagaste
stops.date_confidence: attested: Confessions IX.11 puts the death in the thirty-third year of Augustine's life, autumn 387, aged fifty-six, and the age is his own statement. New Advent gives 387; the English Wikipedia article gives 388. The month here is a placeholder
stops.campa: Five days after the window she takes a fever, and nine days after that she is dead, fifty-six years old, a long way from the tomb she had prepared for herself beside her husband at Thagaste. She tells them to lay her body anywhere and only to remember her at the altar of the Lord. Augustine keeps his eyes dry through the funeral, because he thinks weeping would be a complaint lodged against God, and afterwards goes off alone and weeps for an hour, over her and over himself. She is buried at Ostia.
suggested_refs: The church of Santa Aurea at Ostia, built over Monica's burial site
sources: New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia, 'St. Augustine of Hippo'

stops.name: Rome, among the monasteries
stops.date_confidence: attested that he spent months in Rome before sailing, per the New Advent biography; the span, roughly late 387 into 388, is not fixed and the date here orders the segment
stops.campa: The crossing is closed to him, by winter or by the civil war and the blockade at the river mouth, and he waits it out in Rome. Here he writes against the sect he spent nine years inside: On the Morals of the Catholic Church and On the Morals of the Manichaeans, the work of a man settling a debt he ran up by persuading his friends. He also goes looking at the monastic houses of the city, men and women living in common under an elder, eating once a day, and takes notes he will use when he builds his own.
suggested_refs: De moribus ecclesiae catholicae et de moribus Manichaeorum, begun at Rome
sources: New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia, 'St. Augustine of Hippo'

stops.name: Carthage, the landing
stops.date_confidence: attested for the year, 388; the month is not recorded
stops.campa: He comes ashore where he once sailed away by night, sixteen years after arriving as a provincial boy on a patron's money. His mother is buried in Italy. He is thirty-three, baptized, unemployed on purpose, and travelling with his son, with Alypius, and with a small company who have agreed to hold everything they own in common. Carthage is still Carthage. The theatres are open, the courts are full, and the rhetoric school he ran for nine years has somebody else standing at the front of it. He does not stay.
suggested_refs: The port of Carthage, point of both departures and both returns
sources: New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia, 'St. Augustine of Hippo'

stops.name: Thagaste, the servants of God, and Adeodatus gone
stops.date_confidence: the community is attested, c. 388-391. Adeodatus's death is not fixable: Wikipedia gives 388, the dossier 389-391, and De magistro supplies only a terminus around 388-389. State it as c. 388-390 and no closer
stops.campa: He sells the family land, gives the price to the poor, keeps the house, and turns it into a community of prayer, fasting, study and common property. Adeodatus is with him, and Augustine sets down a dialogue between the two of them, On the Teacher, in which the boy's answers are the boy's own, at sixteen. His wit terrified me, the father writes. Then the boy dies, somewhere in these years, and no source of any kind records the day. Of the death Augustine allows himself a single line: quickly did You remove his life from the earth.
suggested_refs: De magistro, the dialogue with Adeodatus
Confessions IX.6
sources: New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia, 'St. Augustine of Hippo'

stops.name: Hippo Regius, the congregation will not let him leave
stops.date_confidence: attested for the ordination, 391, per Britannica, New Advent and Wikipedia. The crowd scene comes from Possidius and the later tradition; forced ordination is a recognised late-antique literary form as well as a real social pressure, and the mechanics cannot be reconstructed
stops.campa: He goes to Hippo, a port on the Numidian coast, to talk a government official into monastic life and to look at a site, taking care to stay out of towns whose bishoprics are vacant, because a famous convert standing in a strange church is a man about to be ordained by force. Hippo has a bishop: the aged Greek Valerius, whose Latin is poor and who is at that moment asking his people for a presbyter. The congregation turns around, sees Augustine, and takes hold of him. He weeps. They read the tears as humility.
suggested_refs: The ruins of the Christian quarter at Hippo Regius, Annaba
sources: New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia, 'St. Augustine of Hippo'

stops.name: Hippo Regius, the garden and leave to preach
stops.date_confidence: attested in substance from the standard biography and Wikipedia's account of Hippo; the month is conventional
stops.campa: Valerius gives him a garden inside the church grounds and lets him found a monastery in it for clergy. Then the old man does something no African bishop does: he lets a mere presbyter preach in his own presence, in his own church, because his Greek accent embarrasses him in Latin and the new priest can talk. The African custom bends, and the men formed in that garden will carry the new habit into their own sees. Other bishops object on principle. Valerius answers that it is done this way in the East.
suggested_refs: The clergy monastery in the bishop's garden at Hippo, seedbed of the Numidian episcopate
sources: New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia, 'St. Augustine of Hippo'

stops.name: Hippo Regius, two days against Fortunatus
stops.date_confidence: attested: 392, from the surviving Acta contra Fortunatum Manichaeum; no month in the reachable sources. The council address of 393 on faith and the creed is folded into this stop for length
stops.campa: The Manichaeans of Hippo are numerous, and Fortunatus, their presbyter, has lived in the town for years and is liked in it. Augustine, who was one of them for nine years, is pressed by Catholics and Donatists together to debate the man in public with notaries taking it down. It runs two days. Fortunatus is driven back onto the question of where evil comes from if God is almighty and good, cannot answer it, says he will go and consult his elders, and leaves Hippo. The following year the African bishops let a presbyter address their council on the creed.
suggested_refs: Acta contra Fortunatum Manichaeum, the stenographic transcript of the debate
De fide et symbolo, 393
sources: New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia, bibliography of Augustine's works

stops.name: Hippo Regius, coadjutor, then bishop
stops.date_confidence: attested c. 395-396: New Advent and Britannica give 395 or 396, Wikipedia gives 395. The disagreement is not resolvable from the reachable sources and both years stand
stops.campa: Valerius, afraid another city will take his priest away, has him consecrated bishop alongside himself, an arrangement that cuts across a Nicene canon forbidding two bishops in one see. Augustine says afterwards that he did not know the canon existed when it was done to him. Valerius dies soon after, and Hippo is his: the church, the poor, the docks, the harvests, the lawsuits, and a see he will not leave again for thirty-four years except to go up the coast to a council.
suggested_refs: The canon of Nicaea against a second bishop in an occupied see
sources: New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia, 'St. Augustine of Hippo'

stops.name: Hippo Regius, the thirteen books
stops.date_confidence: attested: composed c. 397-400 per the New Advent bibliography; Wikipedia gives 397-398
stops.campa: A bishop of two years, answering people who want to know what sort of man they have been given, he writes his life as a prayer: thirteen books addressed to God in the second person, of which nine tell a story and four do not. He puts in the pears, the woman he sent away, the nine years in the sect and the exact shape of his ambition, and he does it in a Latin so worked that the confession is also a performance. He knows that as well, and puts that in too, in the tenth book, where the story has already stopped.
stops.quote: You have made us for Yourself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in You.
stops.quote_source: Augustine, Confessions I.1, tr. J. G. Pilkington, NPNF First Series vol. 1
suggested_refs: Confessions, thirteen books, composed at Hippo c. 397-400
sources: New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia, bibliography of Augustine's works

stops.name: Hippo Regius, the bishop's court and the bishop's table
stops.date_confidence: attested in substance from Possidius's Vita Augustini and Augustine's own letters; the date orders the segment and marks no single event
stops.campa: The work is not the books. Mornings he sits as a judge, because Roman law lets litigants bring a case to a bishop and they would rather have him than the magistrate, so he hears boundary quarrels and inheritance quarrels until noon, hating it and refusing to stop. He ransoms captives out of church plate, dictates letters by the hundred, and preaches oftener than the stenographers can keep pace with. Possidius, who lives in the house and will write his life, records what was on the table and how the talk at it was governed.
stops.quote: I fear not the uncleanness of meat, but the uncleanness of lust.
stops.quote_source: Augustine's own words from Confessions X.31, quoted back by Possidius, Life of Augustine ch. XXII, tr. Herbert T. Weiskotten (1919)
suggested_refs: Possidius, Vita Augustini, chs. XIX-XXII, on the household and the audientia episcopalis

stops.name: Hippo Regius, compel them to come in
stops.date_confidence: attested: Letter 93 to Vincentius, dated c. 408 per the New Advent listing of the correspondence. The Circumcellion violence in the background is standard scholarship and was not in the verified pool; it is flagged as such in the report
stops.campa: The Donatist schism has run a hundred years. Most African towns have two bishops, two altars and two baptisms, and armed bands on the Donatist side burn farms and blind Catholic clergy with lime. Augustine had held, and written, that nobody should be forced into the unity of Christ. He changes his mind in a letter to Vincentius, and gives his reason plainly: it worked. Whole towns came over under pressure and are glad of it now. He takes his warrant from a parable, a master sending a servant out to the highways and hedges.
stops.quote: Whomsoever ye shall find, compel them to come in.
stops.quote_source: Augustine, Letter 93 to Vincentius, NPNF translation, quoting Luke 14:23
suggested_refs: Epistula 93 to Vincentius, the cogite intrare letter
sources: New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia, listing of the correspondence

stops.name: Carthage, the Conference of 411
stops.date_confidence: corrected: the conference sat at Carthage in June 411. The imperial commissioner Marcellinus presided and decided; Augustine did not preside, contrary to the chronology lens. The bishop counts are standard scholarship and were not in the verified pool
stops.campa: The emperor Honorius orders both churches to argue it out once and be done. Hundreds of bishops from each side come to Carthage and stand for the sessions, because the tribune Marcellinus will not have anyone seated. Augustine drafts the Catholic case and does most of the speaking. The case is that the holiness of a sacrament belongs to Christ and not to the minister, so a church full of sinners is still the church. Marcellinus rules for the Catholics, and the confiscations and exiles that follow are enforced by the state.
stops.quote: The glorious city of God is my theme in this work, which you, my dearest son Marcellinus, suggested, and which is due to you by my promise.
stops.quote_source: Augustine, City of God I, preface, NPNF translation, addressed to the same Marcellinus who presided at Carthage
suggested_refs: The Gesta Collationis Carthaginiensis, the official record of the 411 sessions
sources: New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia, 'St. Augustine of Hippo'

stops.name: Hippo Regius, the two cities
stops.date_confidence: attested: begun 413, completed c. 426, twenty-two books, per the New Advent bibliography
stops.campa: Rome has been sacked by Alaric's Goths and the refugees are in Africa saying this is what comes of shutting the temples. Augustine answers with twenty-two books over thirteen years: ten demolishing the claim that the old gods ever protected anybody, twelve building a history of two cities founded on two loves, the love of self to the contempt of God and the love of God to the contempt of self, mixed together in this age and sorted only at the end of it. In book sixteen he pauses to rule that the dog-headed men of the geographers, if they are rational and mortal, are sons of Adam.
stops.quote: the earthly city, which, though it be mistress of the nations, is itself ruled by its lust of rule
stops.quote_source: Augustine, City of God I, NPNF translation
suggested_refs: De civitate Dei XVI.8, the ruling on the monstrous races
De civitate Dei XVI.9, the denial of the antipodes
sources: New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia, bibliography of Augustine's works

stops.name: Hippo Regius, the long war over grace
stops.date_confidence: attested: the controversy runs from 411 to his death and the Contra Iulianum opus imperfectum is unfinished when he dies. The date here orders the segment and marks no single event
stops.campa: A British ascetic named Pelagius has been teaching at Rome that a man can keep the commandments if he decides to, and Augustine, who could not decide for years and knows exactly how long, spends nineteen years answering him. Grace comes first, unearned; infants are baptized because they are already inside the fault. Rome condemns Pelagius, then unmakes the condemnation, then remakes it under imperial pressure. Julian of Eclanum, young and merciless, keeps the fight going long after Pelagius is finished, and calls Augustine a Manichaean still.
suggested_refs: Contra Iulianum opus imperfectum, left unfinished on the desk in 430
sources: New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia, bibliography of Augustine's works

stops.name: Hippo Regius, going back through everything he wrote
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Retractationes are dated 426-427 in the New Advent bibliography
stops.campa: At seventy-two he goes back through his own works in the order he wrote them, from the Cassiciacum dialogues forward, and lists what he now thinks is wrong with each one. He does not revise the texts. He leaves them standing and appends the corrections, book by book, so that the mistake and the retraction travel together in the same volume. He assumes his errors will be copied and read whether he approves of them or not, and works on that assumption. No other ancient author left such a catalogue. Two books, finished in 427.
suggested_refs: Retractationes, two books, 426-427
sources: New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia, bibliography of Augustine's works

stops.name: Hippo Regius, the psalms on the wall
stops.date_confidence: attested: 28 August 430, during Geiseric's siege, per Britannica and New Advent. The deathbed detail comes from Possidius, who was in the city and probably in the room
stops.campa: Geiseric's Vandals hold Numidia and the refugees are inside the walls; the siege is in its third month. Augustine takes a fever and stops receiving anyone but his doctors and whoever brings food, so that nothing will interrupt him. He has had the penitential psalms of David copied out in large sheets and hung on the wall facing the bed, and he lies there reading them and weeping freely and constantly, ten days, seventy-five years old. Possidius, watching, had already written down what the bishop asked God for a few months earlier.
stops.quote: I would have you know that in this time of our misfortune I ask this of God: either that He may be pleased to free this city which is surrounded by the foe, or if something else seems good in His sight, that He make His servants brave for enduring His will, or at least that He may take me from this world unto Himself.
stops.quote_source: Augustine during the Vandal siege of Hippo, reported in Possidius, Life of Augustine, tr. Herbert T. Weiskotten (1919)
suggested_refs: Possidius, Vita Augustini, ch. XXXI, on the last illness and the sheets on the wall
sources: New Advent Catholic Encyclopedia, 'St. Augustine of Hippo'

stops.name: Cagliari, the body carried out of Africa
stops.date_confidence: corrected: the afterlife lens dated this to the 500s, but Huneric reigned 477-484, so the expulsion and the translation belong to c. 484. The church of deposit at Cagliari is named in no reachable source, so the pin is the city and nothing finer
stops.campa: Fifty years after the siege the Vandal king Huneric expels the Catholic bishops of Africa in their hundreds, and they carry the body across to Sardinia with them. The bishop of Hippo leaves Hippo for good in the baggage of exiles. Where in Cagliari they laid him is not recorded anywhere; the sources give the city and stop. From this point the itinerary is no longer his own, and every move afterwards is somebody else's decision about a box of bones.
suggested_refs: The Vandal persecution under Huneric, 477-484, and the exile of the African episcopate

stops.name: Pavia, San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro
stops.date_confidence: traditional: dated to around 720. Bede is the earliest witness usually cited for the translation and his text could not be reached in this pass, so the Peter and Liutprand chain rests on modern secondary summary alone
stops.campa: Saracen raiders are working the Sardinian coast, and Peter, bishop of Pavia and uncle of the Lombard king Liutprand, buys the relics and has them brought north to the Lombard capital, into the church called Saint Peter in the Golden Sky. The church around him will be rebuilt, sacked, suppressed and rebuilt again, and he stays inside it through all of that except for one century. Augustine is Lombard property now, thirty-odd kilometres from the Milan where a vintage holiday once gave him his excuse to quit.
suggested_refs: The Basilica of San Pietro in Ciel d'Oro, Pavia

stops.name: Pavia, the marble ark and the box of bones
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Arca di Sant'Agostino was carved 1362-1365 by Giovanni di Balduccio. The 1695 discovery and the 1728 ruling of Benedict XIII are separately attested and folded into this stop; the 1785 expulsion, the 1799 move to Pavia Cathedral and the 1896 reinstallation belong here too
stops.campa: Giovanni di Balduccio carves the tomb: three tiers of white marble, more than a hundred and fifty figures of angels and saints and bishops, and relief panels running the life from the pear tree to the siege. In 1695 workmen open the floor and find a marble box holding bones, fragments of wood, and glass vials. Two branches of the Augustinian order dispute for thirty-three years whether these are the right bones. In 1728 Benedict XIII rules that they are. No chain of custody runs from the box back to Hippo, and the ruling is an ecclesiastical one.
suggested_refs: The Arca di Sant'Agostino, Giovanni di Balduccio, 1362-1365

stops.name: Annaba, the arm in the glass tube
stops.date_confidence: attested: the cubitus was brought from Pavia in 1842, and the basilica was built 1881-1900 and consecrated on 29 March 1900, not 29 April as the afterlife lens had it. The pin is the basilica's own coordinates from the French Wikipedia article, correcting two wrong values in the pool
stops.campa: A piece of the right arm comes back. French colonial Algeria wants a shrine on the hill above the ruins of Hippo, and Pavia gives up a cubitus, sealed into a glass tube and set inside the arm of a life-size marble figure of the bishop lying down. The basilica rises around it between 1881 and 1900 to Joseph Pougnet's design, banded, neo-Moorish, visible from the sea, and is consecrated on the twenty-ninth of March 1900. From its terrace the excavated foundations of his own church are a short walk downhill.
suggested_refs: The Basilique Saint-Augustin d'Annaba and the recumbent statue holding the cubitus

stops.name: Souk Ahras, the olive tree
stops.date_confidence: no date: the landmark is present-day and this date only closes the sequence. Reported as a negative finding, Wikipedia, 'Souk Ahras', which documents no monument or museum to Augustine in his birthplace beyond a listed tourist landmark
stops.campa: In the town that was Thagaste there is no museum to the man born here, no monument, and no statue. The tourist listing names one landmark, the olive tree of Saint Augustine, and says nothing further about it: not its age, not who first attached the name to it, not whether anyone still goes. The birthplace keeps a tree, and the written record keeps nothing else. The house where Patricius counted his few fields is somewhere under a modern Algerian city.
suggested_refs: The landmark known locally as the olive tree of St. Augustine, Souk Ahras
